You were talking about the five minute dance, is that a barred dance or something?

Well yeah, that's when a guy got a break. And more likely, well that's the time most of us would use the music. In other words, we'd use the music but we wouldn't play nothing maybe but the chorus. You see? Then we had a chord with all the head numbers so you wouldn't get confused, you know what I mean? You'd look on the chord and see what number you want to play and then you had the music to play. Now it's never if you're gonna play five minute walls, but then we would play instead of like we used to have the music repeat the second ending. You just make introductions, keep straight on down. And by that time you do it, five minutes be up, you see? How long did the other numbers last?
Well the other numbers. Was it time or just the chord or number?

No, it depends. If you played a slow number, if you ain't play no more than two chords, fast or slow. Two chords. But when you play the five minute dance, that's the time you would get a chance of a piece of music you like, a song you like. Well then you'd play that all the way. By all the way that means play everything but just don't repeat, just go on down with it. You see? You see? You make the first ending and come back, you know how the music goes. You skip the first ending, make the second ending, go on down and go out with it. You see? That's the way that was operated. Then we played a lot of waltzes and we played a waltz and did the same thing. I took up first chord, the saxophone, rest. Did you play mostly the
popular numbers that day or did you ever play Dixieland numbers like say Tiger, Rack and

Andamore and all those? Yeah, we played them too. We played them too. We played them too. But more likely we played all those places. They would buy the music. They'd buy the music for you? They give the money to a certain one in the band. They go to Royal Irons and each week we get what five or six new numbers. Let me see. Get orchestrations or just-
Orchestrations? No, no. For everybody. How many players do they have? About five or six in the band? Six of them. Six. At the
La Vida was Jim, Paul Barnes, Sidney Fleischer on guitar. Robert Davis on drums and Bennett Turner on piano which is a real good musician.
What happened to Turner? Is he still around? Does he play? I haven't heard of him.
Well I haven't seen him in a long time but he's a good musician. Well he's the one to go
by the music. Go by the music. You're the guy Louie on Lutzenz. Did you ever play Lutzenz?

Oh Lutzenz? Who's that? The Jew, everybody's that. Yeah. I played all out there. And in fact, I mean I've been a lot of places on the early start. I used to, one week I'd be on the Gulf Coast, next week I'd be going to Meridian, and Harrisburg, Poplarville, Picayune, all them places like that slide out. You know one week we'd go to this place, next week then we'd go to Mobile, Pensacola, Florida, and back into Biloxi, Gulf Coast, Paris Christian, Bay St. Louis.
How did you travel usually in the United States? Well, we had cars.

People had some of those type of cars. Yeah cars, you see. All we would have we'd rent them, see. Yeah. Rent the cars. And then we, when I'd taken up with Isley Morgan, they had a truck. We'd just travel the truck. Couldn't go. It was 25 miles an hour.

But we were slow by the show. Well I'd have to sit in the back of the truck then. Yeah, we'd be in the back of the truck. And just go on the road. Let's see if there's anything else about the dance halls we could talk about. About how many girls did they usually hire there?

Over at the dance hall? Yeah, like the Vito. Well they have maybe about 25 or so like that. And they got, I think they, I'm quite sure they got half of the ticket. See, the guys come up to the ticket box and they buy it and they think you gotta give it to the girl. Yeah, every dance. Every dance, yeah. Well that's the way that would do it. And then they'd check in when it's time for them to get off, you know. And then they split it down. That's through Heffers Day.
Those were all, both of those places and the other one on Carondale after all for whites.

Oh yeah, all white. Did they ever have any colored zip in the dance? No, no. They tried it one time upon Ramport and Julia. Didn't go. Didn't go, no. They got him ten cents to dance. He'd never make it. No, they did try it one time. I don't think that, I don't think that, I don't think it lasted over a week. It wouldn't pay. No, they didn't go after that.
Anything else about it? Anything else that happened at those dance halls as much as you can think of?
Well, a lot of times they had like anything else. They had some fights sometimes, you know what I mean? They had a ball like that sometimes. And other than that, everything was alright.
Did they last pretty long in the same management? Did they go broke right off in there? How long did you play the music?
Well, no. Everyone that I know of that worked for, they still stayed in business.
They stayed in long time. They must have made a lot of money. Who patronized? Mostly the sailors and seamen off of the boats? Or who would go?

Well, you know, we could tell who they was. Sometimes you know who they was or you know who they was in there. Well, they had a lot of people, or regular citizens. American would come down and they'd get with them. Well, you know what I mean? You know how that goes. You see?
I just wondered because mostly if they were out of town people and fellows that didn't know where to pick up a girl or how it would be.

Well, if they had a lot of things like that too. A lot of sailors and so forth would come in. Different things. But you'd see a regular civilian would be in there. You see? A lot of people they play the slow ones. They play the slow ones. They come up and say, yeah, so you're playing the slow ones. You know what I mean? Yeah. Well, they drop something on you. Make more than five minutes. Yeah.
You understand, Bill?
Yeah.
You know what I mean? Yeah.
Because you'd be surprised when you go in the back and see what happened.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well, that's the slow ones that made the slaves slow, slow. Yeah. And everybody get together.

Yeah. But for our people, man, no, they don't go for that. They don't go for no ten cents to dance, man. No. Ain't gonna play. I see. You were talking more about the Sam Morgan or Isaiah Morgan bands.

What kind of a band? They made some records. I mean, when you played with them, what type of music did they play? They made some records of some spirituals for one thing. Yeah. Well, I was playing trumpet when they made that. I was in that place. I had my own band. You see? I just wondered, when you were a member, what type of music they played?
Well, they played the Red Book numbers and they had some pretty good musicians there. Yank was playing trombone. Well, full shade. Some of the rag down numbers too.

Yeah, they played, yeah. I wondered because the first time you made your records you played the Climax Rag, which I've never heard of you before. Yeah. You seem to know all those old numbers. I know, man. Some of those with the Morgan Band things.
Yeah, well, yeah, but Morgan Band, well, Sam never, how they played the rough trumpet, he was on the sweet side.

He was on the sweet side. Yeah, he was sweet, straight, and he was on the right. Straight, sweet. Did they have an unusually good beat? A lot of people thought it was a wonderful dance band. It was a wonderful dance band.

Alfred Williams, you know Alfred Williams, he was the drummer. Rudolph was the drummer. And Roy, Roy Evans, he's dead long while. Well, he had some good men. Little Jim was like I told you, he was playing bass. Then after, Big Jim played, but Yank, he played at that time.
How does Yank play? I never know anything about him, never hear much of anybody mentioning him hard of that.

Well, Yank was a good trombone player. He was no high played man. You know what I mean, you know, way up there, but except right in that tradition, he could read too. So Yank played, and his brother played trombone too.
You hear more about him, with your gang, I wonder if it was Yank.
Well, Yank was fine, trombone man. Trombone. Fine, trombone man, yeah.
Was he as good as Buddy in your clothes, or?
Well, different style? It was a different style, first I feel about it. That's the way I feel about it. To me, if they had to hire, I would rather hire Yank. You know what I mean?
Yeah.
It's like the style and feeling.
They both made slide, I guess, all the time. Do you remember any of these vowel trombones when you were a kid? Did somebody play vowels?

Well, I never known a guy that played, but I have seen it because I have played on a vowel trombone, because it's the same thing like the trumpet, you see? And it's like the E flat bass tuba. I play, when I was waking at the farm with Morgan, under Morgan, Andrew Morgan, I used to bring the trumpet and the bass, the straight up bass tuba in place. I play, because it's the same thing. And all the difference is the mouthpiece. I mean, another way you pronounce the notes different, but things the same thing. When I play, it's a play. But I was, you know, when you're young like that, I play it, pep, energy. I think we better move those boys over there. Live! Live! Come to the bass.
I don't think the birds were too loud for that, but we can hear better enough. See, we were talking about the band of the bass and the other bands.

Yeah. Well, yeah, well, I used to play the bass and the vowel trombone, they had some, I don't know, I just remember his name, back in the middle 20s or something like that. But at vowel trombone, the only difference was the mouthpiece. You see? Yeah, that's right. They all, they all, they all, they come out the same way, like the trumpet. See? And then, in other words, you don't find many bass tuba players in New Orleans, fool with no double beat. No, it's not.
They don't play with that. I'm thinking about the Morgan band again. Somebody told me they used to use the slap sticks that Sam and some of them might have
been. Yeah, I have one in there, I use it with George's band. Really?
I never saw anybody do it with George's band. No. Kid Thomas does it over across the river.
I've got the slap stick in there somewhere, right? No, it's someplace I've been there.
Is that sort of part of the trumpet's job sometimes to play that?

Well no, but you see, now Sam Morgan, he used to use that slap stick because he was a funny man about that time. He don't, when he set that tempo, he want the drummer to stay right there and then he'd take that, it'd be the same thing like with a guy, the record and the band, but he'd be with that stick and he got to stay with that stick. That slap stick. Yeah. Well I used to use it, but when we was in San Francisco, at the Hangover I don't know. Well you did all the time, I never used it.
You ever used that? Yeah. I used it. I never saw you do it.
Yeah, well I used it, I used it, but I stopped using it after some people at Lawrence knew, out there, they say you can't hear the banjo, you can't hear that with that slap stick, so.
Well since you don't have a banjo, why don't you take it to England with you? They have a lot of fun. You know I could do that.
Yeah, I could do that.
Yeah, you got something there Bill. Yeah, that'll make a sensation man.

Yeah, man that slap stick, but you can't because, I mean when you do that, you got them, you got them covered. You got them covered. Ladies, do you know where that slap stick at there? What? Do you know where that slap stick? You might know.
Yeah, don't put that with your arm, maybe you can get it in the case, I don't know, maybe put it in the case. I put it in my grip. In the grip, that doesn't take too much room.
No, that's a little bit of tape.

Half a pound and. And I used to. You had some fun, they'll like that over there, I'll bet you they'll like it. Yeah, I could try it. Because I've seen people go over here to Kid Thomas' and they'll ask him how it's made, and they'll look at it and make one like it. So, you know, here's that.
Well I had a guy in Los Angeles, uh-oh, tried to buy it from me. Sure. I was using it at that time. It's inaugurated, wasn't it? Yeah, that's the thing, you want something different.
The drummers used to use it but to have a trumpet player use it.
Now another thing I used to play, you remember the song whistle? Oh yeah. I used to play that real good. Yeah.
Fun. Yeah that was fun too. I know, play all that kind of stuff.
But when I was fooling my dad, I was fooling my dad, I was playing the drums then I was fooling my dad.
Did anybody else in the Sam Morgan band do that with the slapstick? No, just him. You got it? He got it.
Huh? He got what? That slapstick. It looks like a big paddle. I don't think you know, I don't think you know what I'm talking about.
It's in there somewhere. Looks like a paddle. She'd have just seen it.
She'd have just seen it, she'd have seen it, she would know but you know.
You should paddle her once in a while and then she'd know what it was. Yeah! That's deep. Oh there's one thing you didn't tell me about, the excursions to Chicago on the train.
Oh.
I heard you used to play that.
Yeah, that was in the late 20s. I was in Chicago, I played Sam Morgan band was the first band.
You weren't there with them? No, no. They had their own band. Yeah. Before you did.

In 28 I think it was, he made the first trip and then I played in the late 28, 29, 30, 31, eight day trip. Eight day trip. Eight day trip. You'd go see. When Sam and them went, they went the long way, hell and then, bicycle road, I see. And then we'd play at the Warwick Hall. Warwick?
I remember that. 47. 47, yeah.
47 and Indiana I think somewhere up there. Yeah, over in there.
Yeah.

And that's the first time that I remember Lewis because when Lewis was here I didn't know him. See, well he came over at the hall and I got to know him. Which is a fine, fine man and a crazy buddy kid.
Yeah, he's nice man.
Yeah, he's a nice man. I'm telling you, Lewis is fine. You can't find a better man than him. No, he's wonderful.
You played on the train going up too then? Yeah. Where did you play? In the baggage? Baggage, that's right.
That's right with Dale City.
In the baggage. Yeah. We were talking to Eddie Morris yesterday and he played on excursion but he said there wasn't nothing like a baggage car, he played in a coach, no dancing. But you did, huh?

I don't remember him going to Chicago. No, but there were different, no trips around different places? Well maybe, no, well I probably, they were going a short distance. But you see, like when we stopped in Jackson, Mississippi, and Melford, and them different places like that, you'd be there for quite a while and then we'd break them down. You see?
You had your full band, six pieces or so, was it good, huh? I see.
I know I had eight.
Eight, big band. Eight pieces, yeah.
The whole band went up there. Yeah, because I had taken Guy Kelly, which was a wonderful band, and I had taken a band, which was a wonderful trumpet man, you heard of him.
You made a couple records.
Well I'm the one taking him to Chicago.
Was that right man?

His people were there, his mother I think, and I dead hit him, you understand, and put a few dollars on him, which he played, you understand, and Poissy, uh, uh. Percy Umphrey. Percy Umphrey. Yeah, Percy Umphrey. He went with me, old man Joe Howard, Eddie Jones with Wicked Widow.
Howard played second trumpet then, not the trumpet. No, no, he played the tuba.
Tuba? Yeah, he played the tuba. He played the tuba, Henry Harden, which he's dead now, he's gone, and Henry. Yeah.
Then you played, you'd have those special dances at the Royal Rick, or did the organization put the, who hired you to go out? Did some be some lodge, or the railroad? No, no, it wasn't no lodge.
It was a guy by the name of Andrew, Andrew Jackson, I think that was the man. Anyway, he waited for the railroad. And the railroad. He put it on a hot, I would be dead. I know that he was head of it.
I have heard of excursions like say the Elks or something would hire a band when they go to a contention. Yeah, but no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. Nothing like that.
The railroad. This guy waited for the people, he was a porter or something on the train, and he made connections some kind of way, and that's the way it would come out. He would hire the band.
Yeah. And when you got to Chicago, how did you get these jobs at the Royal Rick, or how was that arranged?
Well, that was arranged by him.
He had that whole thing. Yeah, he had all that, all that street. One big deal.
Yeah, see, well he knew all that, but I think he was working out from that, some kind of way he knew how to make the connection.
That'd be just open to the public, anybody go in there and see?
Anybody be at the door. And I mean the people from here, the people come leave from here on the excursion, well.
When you'd be there four or five days, how many nights did you work up there?
I work up maybe about two nights, that's all. About two nights, that's all.
Somebody told me once you played on a wagon up there at Adrigan. Yeah, that's the time, yeah. How was that? I never heard all that.
Man, man, that was the time. That's the time, Lee was waking up at their story up on Ramport Street, and they went for some other people. And anyway.
Well, Lee wasn't living up there then. No. He was from here. No, he was here. Because he had been up there and he's there now.

Yeah, but I, no, no, Lee was here. He was playing on that story. Yeah. And anyway, so we got out there, the two trucks, and we tied up on 47 and I think in, where the Riggle Theater at? South Parkway. Well, 47 and South Parkway. South Parkway, man, they never seen something like that in all their life. Boy, we tied up like we did back there in the olden days. And Bill, did we have a ball? And that's when Punch, Punch Miller, well he had been up there pretty good while. Punch Miller, we call him Kid Punch right here. Well, he came and he jumped on the truck because it looked like a person was kind of afraid of them people, you know what I mean?
And he jumped up there and, you know, got on the truck and- And played with me.
Yeah, yep. Because Lee was really so much sad.
Yeah, man, people like that, Ethel Warwick, all the people was around. Sure, all the the-ethical people. Yeah. Yeah, the-ethical people.
Yeah, man, man, boy, street was, they never seen that thing in all their life. And we stayed there for hours.
Is that the advertiser dance at the Warwick?

Yeah, that's right, the advertiser, I just remember where they were playing. They were playing other bands. Yeah, they were playing some other plays, that's right. And man, we had a sub-bomb. Oh, man. Yeah, we went all over Chicago on the trucks. And you just stay like we used to do, you know, and they just went from one corner to the mix. Stop up there, you play, I play, you play, I play, and that's the way the thing went. You see?
The big signs on your truck? Yeah. For sure. Of course. They sell any tickets in advance off of the truck or anything?
No, no, no, I wouldn't sell no tickets. There's no way it was that at all.
Any other cities that you got to, like New York or Cincinnati in those days? Those old days?
No, no, no, I never go.
Never go to California except in late years?
Late years, that's all. No.
What about any other, aside from Mobile, Mississippi, did you ever get up to Shreveport or? No, I never go to Texas. No, I never go to Texas.

All the time I went to Texas when I was George, then I went to Fort Worth and passed through Texas, you know, but mostly out of Mississippi and Alabama, see, or New Ibarium, some of them places like that, you know.
Yeah, no time is very close to you.
No, I never go to the west too much.

I was going to ask about a few of the other old time trumpet players since you probably, did you watch mostly the drummers when you were a kid or what interests you most, drummers or the trumpet players?

Well, I always wanted to be a trumpet player from a kid. But like I told you, I finally wanted to tell them that I could play the drum and I got jammed up there and I had to get up there and do something. So I started to play the drum. But the trumpet was what I always wanted. But the part was about the thing, just like driving an automobile. And nobody showed me to drive an automobile. I sat there and looked and I see the guy, what did he do? So I'd get in there and go do that. You see, the same thing with the drum. I'm looking at it, what did he do?
So that was it.
I didn't make no mess up or nothing of that sort.
In the old days when you started or even before when you watched the drummers, did they most of them use a four beat or a slower two beat bass drum?

Well, it depends on the tune he was going to play. It's a number. See, now if they're going to play well, if they beat that one beat like that. See? Now, like a lot of drummers right now, I know that's the way you're supposed to play. Yeah, I'm talking about that. But if you get tired, you can ride it, but you got to know what you're doing, you're going to ride it like that. You know what I mean? Well, that's the time of your rest. That's all the rest period, you see? But I can't change it in that quick for the keep up.
Yeah.
You see?
But, yeah, that's right. Like that. Just use your whole leg. That's right. It does make it a little easier in this. Yeah.
Well, and a lot of real drummers that play in it every day, they beat from their toe.

Yeah. You see? Yeah. In regard to some of the early, Thomas, do you remember King Oliver, or Joe Oliver as they call him? No. Did you ever hear him when you were a kid? No. He left, I guess, when you were ten years old. I imagine.
He should have been. I don't know anything about him.
Do you ever remember hearing Keppert anything?
No. Never heard Keppert. No, I played Buddy Petit. I met him.
You asked about him.
Yeah, Buddy Petit. Well, I played his film at Louis Armstrong, we're here at the Suburban Garden, 1930 or 31, between that time.
About 31 I believe.
I think in 31 he was here. And he was Paul Bell and I played Buddy Petit's film.
How many bands did they use?
They had two. They had the Eureka band and I had my brass band.
How big was your band then in those days? Ten. About ten. About ten. About ten. About the same, did you use saxes then or clarinet and alitoes or what did you use?

Well, we were at clarinet and I just remember all the fellas, it's been so long time before. Twenty years. But I know George was there. Jim was there. Little Jim at that time, he was playing the tuba. Playing the tuba. Yeah.
I heard him even a couple years ago. He was still there.
Well I mean he was on the street with me. And at that time when I had met Buddy maybe about five or six years before he died. And when he really was playing all that trumpet and stuff like that.

What style did he play? I mean can you describe it? I mean I know you can't go into great detail without actually playing the part and trumpet. I mean did he use much mute work like Chris Kelly or was it mostly open?
No, no it was open.
Just about all of them.
But now he was no high note man but. He might turn this to him. Huh?
Let's close this a little bit too. He was no high note man.
He wasn't high note though? No but he was a trumpet player.
Was he a sort of rough or sweet style or what?

Sweet but good. Good. See when I met him, first time I met him it was in Bugalusa. Yeah. Bugalusa. And he was playing a lot of horn then. After that he came back home here and played a trumpet. No way he wasn't too much with that mute. I mean he didn't use that, he played, but he could fingers so good. Yeah.
Did he play very loud or soft mostly or what was it? Very?
No he could go loud and get soft in any way. He had a fine tongue, something like bunk. Yeah.
See?
But he could finger that thing. And he played everything in the Red Book. We called it Red Book all the numbers that he played all of that.
Yeah. Did he read much or used music never? Well I don't know, I wouldn't know about his reading ability. Naturally he wouldn't have the music much on the job I guess.
No I don't know if they'd have somebody that worked with him, you see, to know that. But I would have played, but I would have played, you know, there ain't no music or nothing like that.
When he played around here was it mostly big dances like at the economy? Sam played in all those places.
Fabio and all those places he played all of that.
Ever played in little dunks like in Connery Bar Rooms and things too? All that goes, sure.
Just everything.
It's like Chris.
Chris played a lot of parties, we used to have parties. People say there are parties on Monday nights at different places. At the house, the house party. Well they have four or five pieces.

Speaking of parties, we'll come back to your buddy McKee again in a minute if I think there's something to ask. Did you ever play many fish fries or lawn parties? Can you tell me anything about those?
Yeah, well like Red Island, all of us played those lawn parties. That's open in the yard.

I went to about two of them is all I ever went to in my life. Did they ever run them? I understand some people like Betsy Cole, Miss Cole's lawn parties uptown had them every week. But some people, did they just put on a party maybe once a summer and have it a lawn party? Or did people have it regular every week at their house or what?

Well the lawn parties, well it depends. Just like right across the street here. They have in the summertime, they have either fish fry or they have a party with music or you know. And that's the way that people rent your yard or foot-a-law and park. Oh yeah, that's right.
Is that the place where they record the Eureka band?
Right across the street.
In there?
Yeah, that's right. I forgot about that. Yeah, that's right across the street. They're about the regular there then. In the summertime, yeah. Still do?
Sure. Who plays those? I never know anything about them.
Well different people who's given it, they hire what they want.
Some good bands sometimes.
Well they have maybe three or four pieces but the noise, you see. And that's the way that goes. Yeah.

I wonder if people hired bands sometimes just like to pay their own rent or something, you know, like in Chicago they used to have these house rent parties. No, no. Were the fish fries ever used for that purpose? No, not that I know.
When the people give us something, they used to have fish fries way back but they have suppers now. You see across the street or they have it in their home, you know that'd be for their own put.
Is it true that the fish fries used to be mostly Saturday night only? Saturday night, that's right.
Only. Only on Saturday night.
That's right. And the lawn parties, when would they be? Any old time?
Well it could be Saturday or Sunday and sometimes they'd have more Mondays, between those three days.
The ones I went to were both Sunday nights?
Well some would have more Mondays or Saturday or Sunday, like I said. What about picnics?
Did you ever play many or go to many when you were a kid? I played a lot of picnics.
I played a lot of picnics this year. We never hear about those usually. In the country? Yeah, in the country. That's where they go.
A year lately they've been going Nine Mile Point. Where is that now? That's right down here in Chile.
Down the lake? Yeah, down in Chile. And La Place. That's been a lot of them up there. A lot of them up there? Yeah. And the pigs?
Where is the pigs? Where is the pigs?
That's right down here in Chile.
Down in the lake?
Yeah, down in Chile. And La Place. That's been a lot of them up there. A lot of them up there? Yeah.
There's room after another question. Did you ever play at Millenburg or go out there?
Yeah. I played Millenburg.
Okay, we're talking about the island of Millenburg. Did you ever play there before they tore it down?

Yeah, I played there when they had all of those camps out there. I played out there with Jake Carey on the drum and I played with my arn band out there in Millenburg. Then I played at a white nightclub out there.
Was there a nightclub? They had a nightclub out there. I thought most of these little camps out over the water.

Oh yeah, well I mean they had camps out on top of that's colored, but I don't know, but we, let's see, a fellow called Hickman, Albert Boyd Banks, Louis Gallo. Louis Gallo played the piano. I forgot we played the drum. Anyway, we played out there on the weekends, quite a while. I played a trumpet then.
Tell me, some people have told me that Millenburg was part colored, or one time it was white and then they changed it to colored, or was there any?
Well I don't know anything about that.
Well I don't know anything about that.

I thought it was colored. I mean at the time. The places you played were colored? No, the one I played, they had a camp out there, a night, I mean not a camp, it was a nightclub. Yeah. And that was strictly for white, and I had to operate when I had a muse at the weekend, you see. Yeah.
And uh. These places out over the water, those were colored people, hadn't they?
Yeah, colored people. Well you see, it's like down Seabrook, out them places, that's where the white camp.
Uh huh. What about the Spanish Fort? Did you ever play there, go out there, any music out there?
Yeah, I have played out there, in different clubs, out in the Spanish Fort, in Bucktown.
Was the Spanish Fort mostly for whites, or was it colored art, or just all white?
Bucktown white.
What about West End? All white. It was all white in your days, because I understood one time it was colored. Well I don't know.
You don't remember when the color.

I don't remember when the color. I heard once back in 1898 or something like that, they changed it from white into colored. And I thought maybe it was colored ever since then or something. I don't know anything about that. When you were young then it was all white? No, I played on all in place, and I was just nothing like that.
Bucktown, that was all white clubs? White clubs.
Bucktown, maybe. That's what I wondered.
Doesn't make too much difference. West End? Yeah. Yeah.

What? When somebody tells me one thing, you know, I never know. Yeah. It might have been before my time. Before my time. So you mentioned Jack Perry. Man, it's been so long. You played drums or? I played drums. Yeah. Was Punch playing with him? Yeah. Was Punch playing with him? Yeah. Yeah.
I was in the band with Jack Perry. Man, it's been so long. You played drums or?
I played drums. Yeah.
Yeah. Was Punch playing with him then, do you think?
No, I don't think Punch was playing. No. But it's been so long, I just can't get that together. See?
But I know I worked out there with him.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I knew his brother much, pretty well. Let me see. I'm quite sure it was Gaudet playing trumpet. What's the name again? Gaudet. Gaudet. I don't see if I can make it anymore. Is he still around?
No, he's dead. I didn't think about it. He died.
He died. He died. He died. He died. He died. He died.
He died. He died. He died.
He died. He died.
He died. He died. He died.
He died. He died.
He died.
He died. He died. He went to live in Los Angeles. And he, I think he died up there if I'm not mistaken.
To get back to Buddy Petit, who did he usually use in his band when you heard him? Did he just have to pick up a group different or some of the records? No, no.
When I heard him over in Burger Lucy, he just, in other words, he was there playing with some fellas.
Never paid too much attention to the others.

No, in fact, I never had a chance to listen to them because most of the time when they were working, we were working at the same time. So we couldn't get to each other that way, you see. And when he came back home, well, he worked it in a way he could get a job or, if he got a job, he just hired some fellas, you know. Stayed there.

Anything else about his funeral? And you say there were two bands for his funeral. That's right. Eureka and your band. That's right. Louis Armstrong, I didn't know what to say. He was a ball player. He was a ball player. He didn't play anything.
No, he didn't play nothing. He just split the body.

Were any of his relatives around that you know? I knew his stepfather, you know, Joe Petit, the trombone player. Did Buddy have any, somebody said he had a brother once, I think they called him Sonny. Do you know any of his relatives?
I do, but now where they live at, I couldn't tell you that. Not long ago I was seeing his brother.
He does have a brother living there.
Wait. Drag knows where Buddy's brother Sonny, but you're talking about Sonny. I know. He lives in the next block from Drag on Begunna Street.
Yeah, I'll ask Drag about that.
Drag, but we know exactly where he live at. I'm sure he do. Because I know I was talking with Sonny about a month ago.
Yeah, I wasn't sure if he was still living. Yeah, he's still living. If he even was a brother, I heard that last year.
Yeah, then he could straighten you much better on Buddy.
On Buddy.
Yeah.

In regard to the old time trombone, who was your favorite? Of course, it's hard to pick one person. Who were the, of all the fellows you've ever heard in your life on trumpet, who did you like best? Probably, I know you talked about doing Armstrong, you just mentioned. Oh yeah. Would he be your favorite or are there other fellows?
No, no. Nobody like Lloyd after me. That's my man. That's my man.
And most people would say that I think too.
I've always loved that he's playing. See, I still do.
Next to him of the other old timers, who would you pick? Well, Chris.
I loved him with that sweet playing with that mute. You see, that was great.

Somebody told me once that, of course I've heard you play Careless Love a lot of times, and you made a couple of nice records of it. Did you ever try, I'm not trying to accuse you of imitating anybody, but I mean did you ever try to sort of play like Chris's?

Well, when I first started and got the band together, I used to play exactly like he played with the mute. I had the wah-wah and everything, and all the time he could tell the difference. When they'd come into the hall, because the Al Jays and all the people was crazy about Chris, and he used to send me on a lot of jobs. Well, they did think it was Chris that would be me playing.
You know what I mean?
But I used to play exactly just everything he played, I played.
But some people told me once that if they heard you play like Careless Love, it was almost like hearing Chris play. Well, I mean, you don't do it that way now though.
No, I mean I have been using that mute, and that wah-wah, that's the way it's got to be did.
You have to do it with that.
See? And then I mean, when I play with the band, they play in a different key. Oh.
What key did that? He played it in F. In F. Mm-hmm.
E flat concert. You see?
And George's band, what key did they use in it?
Well, they used it in G for the trumpet. Of course, I couldn't make it, but I made it.
No way.
And the way he used to play it, he started off the blues. The drummer would give two beats with the stick on the bass drum. Boom, boom.
Then he's da-da-da-dum, boom, boom, da-da-dum, boom, boom, da-da-da, da-da-da, da-da-da,

ba-boom, da-da-da, the drum organ. Then after he'd get it played maybe two, three chords, then he'd go to ta-da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da, you understand? They'd come into the Callous Love, and then he'd get that act tape.
But he didn't use the newt all the way through then?
No. No, no.
He only used it when he comes to the Callous Love. The Callous Love part.
When he comes to the Callous Love part, then, anyway.
He played the first part all over then.
All over.
That's right.

That's right. That's right. But you could tell him before, I mean, anywhere people come, they could tell him. I used to do, that he had a way to do with the horn before he started, you know, to start the band. He'd just run over the horn and all that kind of, da-da-da-da, ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba. And he'd keep doing something like that, one of those things until he got rid of the knock the band off.
I see. Is it that they were practicing sort of? Well, no.
It just, well, no. At that time, they didn't have a union and stuff like that. The fellas might be scattered around in a wholesome place. He called them. He was calling them.

He was calling them. Yeah, that's what, that's what. So maybe it was sort of like these warming up, you know, or- No, no. You also just had so much music in him, he had to keep playing all the time. No, no.

No, no. It would get the fellas together. I got them together. See? And I mean, like you play a number, you play like that, and that guy play a number two, then everybody take a walk. Of course you had to go from eight to two or something like that. It was long hours, but, and then at that time, when I come, I come along in the, in the, in the, in the kind of, uh, last part of the thing, but, uh, the, uh, at 12 o'clock, you come off the stand, everybody, and sit at a table long under this, and have something to eat. I don't make no sandwich.
Mm-hmm. It's like regular, uh, big balls, like- Big balls, kind of, all of them places.
You come down, and everybody eat, and drink. That's for free. At 12 o'clock.
12 o'clock.

You come down and eat, and we still have those bunkies on Monday. That's plenty of, all that playing like the fellas playing now, and I don't know where they get that stuff but standing up for the Dixieland. You get to sit down. Everybody sit down.
Everybody sit down.
You stand up if you're going to take a solo or something. Mm-hmm. I think that's true.
There wasn't no standing up proposition.
But I know, what I'm talking about, they're representing the Dixieland business and the, that, that old time jazz, but there wasn't nobody standing up.
No, that's-

I don't understand that book. Burst, Burban Street, isn't it? It must be. But there wasn't no such thing. When we went to New York to play at Charles Brammer, that they want to put seats up there first. I said no. Joyce said no, standing. I said, well, God, a boy, you, all of them, this is not.
I don't know how to do it. You can relax more except for families, right? I know you can. You see.
But that, that's the way, that's the way it is now. You have to keep it going that way.

Well, in those old days, like at the economy hall, there are different halls, did they play more blues after midnight, I've heard, than the old days they did sometimes? They saved most of their blues until late at night?

Well, they saved more of the blues until people get crowded in there. And then you worked it like that. You could work it easier. And I mean it's like out there, they didn't play Panama all night long with all that fancy music. They played waltz, blues, popular numbers would come out, they played all that. But the majority of the people, now they guys are kind of funny, they think you got to just play Panama and Tagore. That ain't that, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, not the way I, the part I know of it. You play a new number, like all the nice numbers come out, who's never could read the band, they go buy the music, and they play it until other guys get on to the number, and play a new number too.
That's right.
I mean, that's, when I was a kid, that's the way it was. But now, if you don't sit there and play when the sins go marching all night long, you ain't nowhere.
You see that baby? I was gonna ask about Manuel Perez, did you ever hear him much?
Yeah, I read him, yeah.
How late did he play? Was he playing much in the 30's? Did you ever see him turn off a little? I wonder, did he play many parades? Did you remember hearing him much on the street or in dances?
Yeah, yeah. Manuel had a musical band.
I never got to hear it, so I don't know what he's talking about.
What? No, a musical band, he never played like we play out the street now. Everything was by music, they played those six eights.
Like the Eureka does sometimes.

They played the six eights, and they played the fuel marches. Played going to get to that body, they played a hymn, maybe when they get near to the place, you know, where the body was. And then they played the fuel marches, when they leave from there, and six eights. Wasn't no rough.
Coming back there from the graveyard, would they ever play, say like Diddy Ramble and all the rough stuff, or did they jazz up the numbers? Well no, not that I know of.

Every time I would, but no, he could jazz. I thought I wanted to be. Yeah, he could jazz, but when they'd be out there they'd be playing that music. They'd be playing that music, like you do now, and all that kind of, you know.
How late did he play around in the streets, and how late did he work with his dance band?
Well about the same thing.
I mean how long since he died, about 1946 I believe, but when did he stop playing? Do you remember when you heard him, how you were?

No, I heard him, I remember he used to play, long years ago, there was different stores, would have a band to play out in front, and so forth like that, and I'd hear him play with six pieces, something like that. Well then he would be playing, you know, jazz, by head or something like that. But when he'd play on the roof guard and all that place up there, the tempo. Oh yeah. Well everybody was reading.

I was wondering if he played much like at the time that you went to Chicago, was he still active as a musician then? Yeah. Still working? Yeah. Yeah. Well 1930, even by Buddy McKee's death, he was still? Yeah, he was playing. Still playing. Mm-hmm. I'm going to ask a little bit about Kid Rene, if you heard him very much, how he played. I even met him and heard him play, but he was not very well when I heard him. Well when you heard him, he was shot up then.
Yeah. But he was wonderful. He was really good. Yeah, really good. I was Paul Barrett for a year when he died.
Now did you ever play with him in any brass bands? Yeah.
Yeah, I played brass bands with him.
Was he mostly high note bands on people of Tony?
Yeah, he could go up there. Clean. Clean, what?
Was it a big tone or sort of small tone? No, no, big tone.
Big tone. Big tone, yeah. A wonderful trumpet man. Clean. Yeah. Could do that.
Do you still prefer Chris Kelly to Buddy McKee and Kid Rene and those other men, Sam Marginal and D. Yeah, Lewis and Chris. And Chris are the two idols favorites. That's mine.
But Rathafell is wonderful.
Oh yeah, sure. Wonderful.
They're wonderful. Very tough. But I like Chris with that mule. Like that.
Some people told me that Chris mostly played like you might say for a rougher crowd, not the society dates so much. Is that true?
Well, I mean a way.
I think that his followers mostly the common people you might say rather than the dicky and ritzy people.

Well no, I don't think he made connection that kind of way because they kept him so busy with those kind of people which you may see. And other words, money, money, and he first come for his soil. Yeah. You see.
He played all sorts of dances.
He played a lot of white dances.
I don't mean necessarily white but I mean color to the woman. I mean like say the Fronson Me Hall. You know, sort of a classic place where they didn't have much rough music or music.
Well I don't know about him playing at the Fronson Me Hall or different places but I know he played all in other places. I know that for sure.

I was going to ask. You know, let's see. I've got a month in here I had now to ask about some of the pieces, the different names of the pieces. Like the other night when you called it, Fidgety Feet, you said War Cloud.
Well yeah, well some say Fidgety Feet, some say War Cloud. But it's the same song. Yeah.
Was that an old number before the fiction? Yes, old number. I always picked it up. Was it a street march or something? Do you think it was on the marches on the street?
You could play it on the street if you want to.
I have heard it on the street. You can play it. You could play it on the street. Play it anyway. The first part has all those clarinet breaks in. I just wondered where it came from.
Well I wouldn't know that part, but I know it's a real old number. It's way back in there.
Did you all have any other names for Tiger Rag?
No, all I know was Tiger Rag.
Some people call it number two Rag and different things. No, I don't know about that.
But I know Tiger Rag.
What about Tin Roof Blues? Is that a...
Tin Roof Blues? That's all I ever know about that was Tin Roof Blues. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.
Yes, sir. Some people, I don't know what they call it, what's that name, because your water's on. Don't get funky because your water's on. Did you ever hear it called that, do you remember?
Yes. Get funky because your water's on, yes. That's the same as the Tin Roof Blues. Yes. They put a pot, put different licks in there. Yes, a little different though.
Yes, that's right. Are there any other, those old time pieces that had some crazy names like that, or some of them that you couldn't even print, you might say?
Oh, yeah.

Most of them, I mean, have... Oh, let's see, somebody, I can't think of... Oh, one of these pieces called something on the tracks or on the rail, all of a sudden. It's on a track. No, I can't think of the name. I was just wondering about some of the other, why did they have those other names for them? Did they have other words, second set of words to those songs, or did they just...
No, as I know, they're the same words. Same words.
That's why they called that water clouds, say, Pitcher Defeat, as an example. No, just some say water clouds or something.
I don't know what reason that they had that, but it's the same song.
You see?
And I said, play fidgety feet, play wall clouds, the same thing. Thanks.

I understand you have quite a collection of music, is that true? I'm not trying to put you on the spot and ask you everything that you know, but I just wondered, I mean I know that you're a musician that knows more tunes than almost anybody around, I understand.

I have up in the front there, a whole lot of music when I had the big band. Willie Pajor and Bill Matthews, the way, with me and the big band. And I have a lot of music. A lot of music. And when Professor John Robichaud died, his wife was Anna, she gave me quite a bit of music. You know what I mean? At that time.
I've had a couple of books of John Robichaud's too with his name stamped on that I got from Maurice Durand or something like that.
That's right. Well, she gave, in other words she gave me half of a gift for Maurice because that was his supplement.
He still has some of them, but I'm in California.

Yeah, I'm in California. That's right. Well, yeah, most of us, when they want something, they come here to me. They go up there and get what they want, bring it back. They got music in there. I'm quite sure I couldn't play a note of it. I've been playing no music for so long. But I used to play. I used to play.
You've got a wonderful memory I know, among other things, the telephone numbers.
Yeah.
If I put my mind on it. You'd probably remember all those too if you'd, all the old numbers too from way back, if you had to play them, wouldn't you?
Well, my property would come to me if I had to play them, you know what I mean? But offhand now, man, you kind of got me.
Yeah. One other question here about the other brass bands that you belonged to. Did you belong to any other brass band when you started, besides from your own band that you led on the street?
I led the Eureka Brass Band. Is that right?
I didn't know you were, you played in the Eureka.

Yes. As Red, Red was playing trombone at that time. Willie Wilson was leading the band. In other words, that was his band, and Johnny Wilson. Johnny Wilson played the baritone. And I went into the band, and after he, and Shots, excuse me.
I remember Shots was in the Eureka band too.
I'm talking about the old Eureka band.
Even before that, yeah.

And, or, or, or, or, or, or, Ornis Rodgers. Yeah. Either one. Got me to come into the band. And, uh, you know, Shots and Wilson, they were talking. A fella, you don't know him, but name called him, Guy Sooner. He's a big, big, big, big, big, big, time guy. You see. And so they was talking about what part to give me. I was just mad at him, Roger, say, give me the part. Don't worry. And that's how I got the band. So anyway, they put me on the first part. Yeah. And I played, and they were surprised. Be taking care of my part. And then they hired me in the band. Well, Shots was always a wonderful second man. He fit for the first part, but he wasn't afraid to give me the solo. And after that, they put me on solo. And from that, they put me to be the leader. And I never would go to the rehearsal in my life. Was never there to come out there. But I was up on it good then. I used to love it, but I don't care for that.
Did you use quite a bit of music in those days? That's what I'm talking about.

That's the part, they had the music. They had the music. Yeah, they used to play the music. And I used to, after Wilson was taking a seat, they put that leader thing on my cap. And I did the band a long time.
Did you play in the Young Tuxedo ever?
Yeah, I played with John, quite a while. Any of the other bands? I played with Eddie Jackson, when he had the original Tuxedo.
His was the original Tuxedo?
Yeah, the original Tuxedo. Yeah. Me Pazzo and Maurice Duran. I was leading that band. Well who else was in that band?
Because I don't know much about them.

Well George was, he worked in the band, and I was leading that band. Was it Celestan? No, Celestan wasn't, give up Eddie Jackson, had the band then. Eddie Jackson, one of the best tuba that we all know ever lived.
I mean in New Orleans.

He was a great guy. You see, he was wonderful. And one of the three trumpets, I know that for sure. Henry Harden played in that band. Earl Fusche played the saxophone. Trombone, man. I believe it was Yanko. Anyway, I know it was good, but everybody was right. It was a good band. Black Happy played. That was a good band. Yeah. That's right. Black Happy played. That, mostly he played.
Oh, now one more question sort of puts you on the spot about who your favorite drummers are, or who they were at all times, not just today. Who was about the best drummer you ever heard? Oh, no.
You got me there.
You got me there. Who did I do? You got me there. I couldn't.
Well, I had some, I had some, I had some, I had played with some, now a fellow like Troy Weiss died, Roy Evans, he was a wonderful drummer.
You see?
Alfred William is a good drummer. Yeah? Yeah.
Well, there's been a lot of good drummer.
No, but George, not George, I mean, Albert Martin, he's a wonderful drummer. I see.
Was it Henry Martin, was he always? Yeah. I used to hear it.
Oh, Henry Martin, yeah, but I mean, at my time when I was coming, I know Henry Martin and Martin and all them fellas, but they wasn't sitting in at that time with Mr. Perry.
Do you remember Red Happy, who used to be a drummer and all that?
Yeah, yeah, at Larry Theater, yeah. Wonderful. He was one of them. Yeah. Zuri, I remember Zuri, but he was at Larry.
Remember him hearing Baby Dodds down here?
No, I never heard Baby down here. I heard him down here after George went to New York with George. Yeah, but I didn't know him before that time.
Remember any other real old timers like Louis Cantrell or Cantrell? Yeah, Louis Cantrell, yeah.
You remember him?
Yeah, I remember him.
Yeah, he's a good drummer, musical drummer.
Remember Mac Murray here?
Mac Murray, oh. Before your time.

Walter Grundy, every year, didn't he? But Walter? He played with the bunk way back, then he took out the taranet. I didn't see it before your time. No, no, I didn't know him. Well, we're just about out of the tape here. Unless there's something else that you want to add?
Well, there ain't nothing else I could say. We're all of the day.

I think, and we might ask if there's any other old-time clarinetists. I mean, we know George, and I've heard all the later fellas, but amongst the old timers, were there any, like George or Boyd? Do you remember him? Yeah.
Good. Good.
Yes, you boy, sure too. Were there any others about that time that are dead that you were your favorites? Oh, Miller Bonds was real good.
One of the good ones. Yeah, he was one of the good ones, too. Zeb. Zeb, I don't know much about his name.
Yeah.
Well, he used to play with Renee.
Was he really good? Do you remember his real name?
All I know was Zeb. That's all it got him. Zeb, something like that.
You played with him then, too, I suppose, at times? Well, yeah, we had played together.
Mm-hm.
Well, I think that covers almost all of your life pretty well. I want to thank you for all . Okay, dear. Okay.

segments.title: Opening tag
segments.summary: Archive tag at the start of the recording.

segments.title: Five-minute dances and how sets were played
segments.summary: Howard explains how the five-minute dance worked, how the band used chord lists and music, and that the hall bands bought new stock numbers each week.

segments.title: Hall band personnel and pianist Bennett Turner
segments.summary: Howard lists the six-piece band's members and says Turner was a good music-reading pianist.

segments.title: Gulf Coast road trips and travelling by car and truck
segments.summary: Howard describes weekly jobs across Mississippi, Alabama and the Gulf Coast, renting cars and later riding in a truck with Morgan.

segments.title: Taxi-dance halls: hostesses, tickets and patrons
segments.summary: Howard describes how dance-hall girls were paid by ticket split, that the halls were all white, who the patrons were, and the slow numbers.

segments.title: Why Black audiences would not pay to dance
segments.summary: A short exchange on what went on in the back and why dime dances would not work for Black patrons.

segments.title: The Sam Morgan band: repertoire and members
segments.summary: Howard recalls the Morgan band's repertoire, Sam's sweet trumpet style, and members including Yank, Alfred Williams, Roy Evans and the Jims.

segments.title: Yank the trombonist compared with another trombonist
segments.summary: Howard praises Yank's trombone playing and says he would hire him for style and feeling.

segments.title: Valve trombone and playing bass tuba
segments.summary: Howard talks about playing valve trombone and the E-flat tuba, which he says are the same as the trumpet apart from the mouthpiece.

segments.title: The slap stick and Sam Morgan's use of it
segments.summary: Howard describes the slap stick Sam Morgan used to hold the drummer's tempo, his own use of it, and taking it to England; he also mentions the song whistle.

segments.title: Chicago excursion trains in the late 1920s
segments.summary: Howard recalls playing in the baggage car on the Chicago excursions from 1928 on, after Sam Morgan's band went first, and meeting Louis Armstrong at the hall.

segments.title: The excursion band and how the Chicago jobs were arranged
segments.summary: Howard names the men he took north and explains that a railroad porter hired the band and arranged the Chicago dances.

segments.title: Playing on trucks in Chicago with Punch Miller
segments.summary: Howard tells how the excursion band advertised the dance on trucks at 47th and South Parkway, with Punch Miller jumping on to play.

segments.title: Other cities he travelled to
segments.summary: Howard says he never went to New York, Cincinnati or Texas in those days and California only in later years.

segments.title: Wanting to be a trumpeter and learning drums
segments.summary: Howard says he always wanted trumpet, taught himself drums by watching, and discusses bass drum beating.

segments.title: Not hearing King Oliver; meeting Buddy Petit
segments.summary: Howard did not hear King Oliver or Keppard but met Buddy Petit.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's funeral and the two bands
segments.summary: Howard recalls playing Petit's funeral with Eureka and his own brass band around 1931.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's trumpet style and playing
segments.summary: Howard describes Petit as an open-horn player, sweet but good, with fine fingering and tongue, who played the Red Book numbers at dances and parties.

segments.title: Lawn parties and fish fries
segments.summary: Howard and the interviewer discuss lawn parties and fish fries, who hires bands and which nights they were held.

segments.title: Picnics, Milneburg and race at the lakefront camps
segments.summary: Howard talks about picnics and playing at Milneburg, including a white nightclub, and whether the camps were Black or white.

segments.title: Spanish Fort, Bucktown and West End
segments.summary: Howard says the places he played at Spanish Fort, Bucktown and West End were white clubs.

segments.title: Playing with Jack Carey and the trumpeter Gaudet
segments.summary: Howard recalls working with Jack Carey's band, thinks Gaudet was the trumpet player, and learns he has died.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's band, funeral and relatives
segments.summary: Howard did not hear Petit's sidemen, recalls the funeral bands, and points to Petit's brother Sonny as a source.

segments.title: Favourite trumpeters: Louis Armstrong and Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Howard names Armstrong as his man and Chris Kelly, with his muted playing, next.

segments.title: Playing like Chris Kelly: Careless Love and the mute
segments.summary: Howard says he once played just like Kelly with the mute and wah-wah, and describes how Kelly started Careless Love.

segments.title: Dance hall customs: eating at midnight, sitting down, repertoire
segments.summary: Howard describes how bands called players together, took a free supper at midnight, sat instead of standing, and played waltzes, blues and popular numbers.

segments.title: Manuel Perez and his reading band
segments.summary: Howard recalls Perez's reading band, the six-eight marches and hymns at funerals, and his dance work.

segments.title: Kid Rena and comparing favourite trumpeters
segments.summary: Howard praises Rena's big, clean tone and again names Chris Kelly and Armstrong as favourites.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's audiences
segments.summary: They discuss whether Kelly played for rougher crowds or society dates; Howard says he played many white dances and everywhere else.

segments.title: Alternate names for tunes: Fidgety Feet, Tiger Rag, Tin Roof Blues
segments.summary: Howard says Fidgety Feet and War Cloud are the same song, and talks about other names for Tiger Rag and Tin Roof Blues.

segments.title: His music collection and the Robichaux music
segments.summary: Howard describes the music he kept from his big band days and the music Anna Robichaux gave him.

segments.title: Joining and leading the Eureka Brass Band
segments.summary: Howard tells how he got into the old Eureka band, was moved to the solo part, and became its leader.

segments.title: Young Tuxedo and Eddie Jackson's original Tuxedo band
segments.summary: Howard says he played with the Young Tuxedo and led the original Tuxedo band under Eddie Jackson, naming its members.

segments.title: Favourite drummers and old-timers
segments.summary: Howard names drummers he admired, including Roy Evans, Alfred Williams and Albert Martin, and says he heard Baby Dodds only later.

segments.title: Old clarinetists, Zeb, and closing
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about early clarinetists; Howard names Miller Bonds and Zeb, and the interview ends.
